associations.name: Chakchiuma
associations.associationType: Historical tribal-group geography in specialist reference
associations.period: Sixteenth-century Spanish-contact records, interpreted by later scholarship
associations.evidenceNote: The article explicitly identifies Sacchuma with Chakchiuma among historic tribal groups in Mississippi named in the Spanish accounts. This supports a Mississippi historical connection while attributing the correspondence to the encyclopedia interpretation.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML body inspected, lines 19–30, especially line 22; limited to the explicit state association and name correspondence.
limits: A geographic connection, not a full Chakchiuma history or proof of a precise town location.
No claim of extinction, modern citizenship, or identity interchangeability with Chickasaw or Choctaw is adopted.

associations.name: Chiaha
associations.associationType: Historical town connection in specialist reference
associations.sourceTitle: David H. Dye — Soto Expedition (Tennessee Encyclopedia)
associations.evidenceNote: Dye places the fortified town of Chiaha on Zimmerman’s Island in the French Broad River near modern Dandridge, Tennessee, in the account of the 1540 expedition. The map record indexes that historical town connection.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML passage inspected, lines 27–32, including the explicit town/state location and subsequent expedition movements.
limits: Chiaha is treated here as a historical town/access point, not as a newly verified present-day tribal government.
The source presents one scholarly location interpretation. Other location proposals and later migrations are not resolved by this record.
No archaeological coordinates or site geometry are supplied.

associations.name: Chipewyan
associations.associationType: Specific present-day First Nations listed in provincial directory
associations.sourceTitle: Government of Alberta — First Nations Relations
associations.evidenceNote: Under its Alberta First Nations introduction and Treaty-territory directory, the province lists Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation and Chipewyan Prairie First Nation. These named governments establish a specific Alberta community connection for the Chipewyan access point.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML introduction, lines 57–62, and Treaty 8 community entries at lines 116 and 119 inspected. Government seat, population and full treaty boundaries were not reviewed.
limits: These specific First Nations do not encompass every community or person represented by the broader Chipewyan name.
This record does not equate all Dene peoples or governments with Chipewyan, or settle preferred names across communities.
The province-wide directory is used for community association, not as a map of exclusive traditional territory.

associations.name: Coca
associations.associationType: Specific community geography in a community-authored published chapter
associations.period: Mezcala community described in a 2017 publication
associations.sourceTitle: Sarah Bak-Geller Corona and Rocío Moreno, coordinators — Recetario coca de Mezcala, Jalisco (Secretaría de Cultura, 2017)
associations.evidenceNote: The government-published volume identifies Mezcala, Jalisco in its title. Rocío Moreno, introduced as a Mezcala comunera and Coca delegate, explicitly identifies Mezcala as a Coca Indigenous community on the north side of Lake Chapala. This supports a Mexico connection through one identified community.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual PDF text inspected: title/publication pages (PDF pages 2–5) and selected opening chapter passages, printed pages 7–9 / PDF pages 8–10. The 81-page volume was not read in full; no recipes or ceremonial instructions were reproduced.
limits: The country index preserves Jalisco/Mezcala in the evidence note; it is not comprehensive Coca geography.
The chapter’s community identity is not invalidated by its discussion of historical language loss.
Contemporary land litigation, ownership boundaries and the present status of projects described in 2017 were not verified.

associations.name: Comanche
associations.associationType: Present tribal government and community location
associations.period: Community-authored public history and headquarters description inspected 2026-10-21
associations.evidenceNote: The Nation’s history describes settlement in southwestern Oklahoma and explicitly places its main headquarters north of Lawton, Oklahoma. These passages directly support a present government/community connection to Oklahoma.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML body inspected, lines 172–178 and address lines 184–186. Only the Oklahoma location statements are used, not demographic estimates or all historical characterizations.
limits: This is one present government/community connection, not a boundary for the full historical Comanche homeland or migration range.
Population figures and broader historical claims on the page were not adopted.

associations.name: Dogrib (Tłı̨chǫ)
associations.associationType: Documented Indigenous language geography and name correspondence
associations.sourceTitle: Government of the Northwest Territories, Education, Culture and Employment — Tłı̨chǫ Resources
associations.evidenceNote: The territorial language overview explicitly locates Tłı̨chǫ’s territorial extent within the Northwest Territories and identifies Dogrib as a historical English exonym used for the language. This supports a carefully scoped Northwest Territories connection for the directory access point.
associations.reviewedScope: Actual HTML Overview, lines 43–49, inspected. Selected language-geography passage only; vocabulary examples and audio were not used as separate evidence.
limits: Language geography is the stated evidence type; it is not a cadastral boundary, modern government jurisdiction or a claim that every speaker has the same political affiliation.
No settlement-agreement terms, population counts or present citizenship rules were reviewed.
